utterances.text: They took pictures of them, of the bomb fragments that fell there. I should do the same, on my way back, and fax them anew should the need arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you there when they took pictures of them?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we got them, we hid them; and upon our return, we did find them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where was it that the pictures were taken? Where were these fragments located when investigators from the Tribunal took pictures of them?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where in Nagavc?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Feim Elshani's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You went to Mr. Elshani's house shortly after this incident occurred of these bombings and explosions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately, but on the following day, in the morning, because when it happened it was 20 to 2.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. Did you see his backyard?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole of the village was there, including the backyard. We did not go inside, though. But on the following day I saw my father's sister, Sajimi Kastrati, there. She had been killed there and I did bury her in the courtyard of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't catch that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any craters from these bombs in Nagavc?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many; do you remember? How big were they?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never measured the size of the craters. All the houses of Nagavc had no tiles on, no roof tiles on. All had fallen down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many craters you saw and about what size they were? That's all I'm asking you about is craters.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea how big they were. But, again, not a single house had its roof tiles on in that village as a result of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the Milosevic trial, you testified on 11 June 2002, at page 6693, and you were asked about this bombing. You said that you had gone there, and then you said this: "But we found pieces of the explosion. We hid them and KFOR took these pieces." That's what you said in Milosevic, that they were taken by KFOR. Today you're telling us they're at this gentleman's house. Which is true?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge is that they are at Feim Elshani's house. Maybe KFOR has taken some of it, but you can get further details on this from Feim Elshani, who came here as a witness on Nagavc. I found and buried children who had been killed in Nagavc, but I haven't spoken about them. I found eight children who had been killed there, all under the age of ten --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nobody is asking you about that. You're being asked about these fragments and you know that, don't you? So please answer the questions you're being asked. Now, my question is this: Why did you tell the Judges, under oath, in Milosevic, that KFOR took these pieces and now you're telling us today that you don't really know whether KFOR took them or not? Why did you tell the Judges that in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: KFOR did take some of it, but there are still fragments from these shells in Nagavc even today. And I have -- I have said it all the time, I've been repeating it, and should the need arise, I will go to Nagavc and take those bomb fragments and bring them over here, as well as the cases that came from heavy artillery shelling on the village. I should bring those as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic asked you yesterday what the Cyrillic letters were that you saw on these fragments and you never answered that question. Would you tell us now what Cyrillic letters you observed?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the Cyrillic letters there. You ought to be able to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where do you think I have them?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can read and write, but I can't read and write in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you don't know what Cyrillic letters were on these shell fragments you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat it: If you need it, I shall bring those bits here and you'll be able to see for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if you know what the letters are that are on these fragments. You can say you don't know; that's okay.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know, but I can't see them here on the screen. I've got nothing in Cyrillic here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, you don't, because I don't have it to show you. But can you tell us what those letters are, or do you not know? What letters did you see on these fragments? If you don't know, say you don't know or you don't remember or whatever.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read that. But I will bring the fragments from these shells here should the need arise, and you will be able to judge yourselves what is written on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I am quite certain that investigators from this Tribunal will want you to show them these pieces and the Cyrillic that's on them. And I'm sure you will cooperate in that regard. Now, you told us yesterday that these fragments were with Mr. Feim Elshani, who had testified in Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Feim Elshani told you about that. We were all present when he did that, again and again, and I will not deny it. I will be able to bring them over here. Not only that, but everything that was fired from heavy artillery, all the casings, I shall bring them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Elshani testified, as you told us, in Milosevic at page 868, and with regard to these fragments, he said that parts of the fragments were handed over to members of German KFOR. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. You can ask him on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Popaj. My name is Djuro Cepic, one of the counsel for General Lazarevic. I would like to go back to your statement from 1999. In paragraph 6 on page 2 of the English, you say that a week before the shelling started -- the bombing started Serb forces arrived, as being the Serbian police and soldiers, about 40 of them at your village. And they began digging trenches on a hill overlooking the village. My question is this: Did those forces come together with some bright orange-coloured jeeps?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't any orange colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The location where the forces were is more or less one kilometre away from your house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one kilometre, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you finish your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not measure the distance, but I don't think it's one kilometre. It doesn't look far away, but if you want to go to that place then it seems to be far.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There is no need for me to go there. I wanted to get an approximate figure of the distance.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not measure the distance. Through the fields it's closer, and if you go there by car it's further.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the 29th of October you spoke to the OTP representatives. You spoke with our learned friend, Ms. Christina Moeller. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On that occasion you said that up to Nahit Fetoshi's house, where the forces were, that that distance is about 900 metres up to one kilometre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said. As I said, I did not measure the distance. I gave an approximate distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Popaj. Let's try and move quickly. I will try to be as clear as possible, and I would kindly ask you for clear answers. You didn't approach those forces; you didn't come close, did you?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went up to the schools because the pupils were still attending school. And from there we could observe them because they were close.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't see any insignia on them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any insignia. As I mentioned, they installed two anti-aircraft cannons, and they expelled Naim Fetoshi with his family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We've already heard that, sir. Thank you. I want to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the court administration to show us P2445.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, do you recognise this mosque?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where it is located.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It used to exist; it does not exist today. It was in Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: On this photograph, it is a bit further away from any other buildings. There are no houses adjacent to it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the middle of the village. This is a road that goes inside the village. There are houses on the upper part and on the lower part, on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. But next to the mosque itself, as we can see on the photograph, there are no family houses?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who took this photograph, but close to the mosque there are houses. And above this road here, there are houses as well. I don't know who took this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many metres away from the mosque are the nearest houses, or used to be?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adjacent to the wall of the yard, and then again on the left and on the right side. Riza is a name of the person whose house is next to the mosque, and Rexhep's house is on the other side here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P1800, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, are you familiar with this location?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Riza's house that was adjacent to the mosque. This is where Rexhep's house was, and this is where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you assert that this is the same location that we saw on the photograph before that?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, what is the point that's involved in challenge to the damage to this particular mosque? What is the point that Defence are making? Has somebody been doctoring photographs or -- bearing in the mind the evidence we've had from Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, quite the contrary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the point of taking time on this? There must be a good for it, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness stated he was present at that time in Celine; that's why we wanted to inquire further as to the events on the 28th of March. And for another reason, and with your leave, I wanted to ask the next question concerning the dates mentioned when the mosques were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, you claim that on the 28th of March the mosques of Bela Crkva, Rogovo, and Celina were destroyed simultaneously; this was your assertion. Before me I have a document, drafted by Mr. Andras Riedlmayer, in which it is stated that the mosque in the village of Rogovo, according to the statements of the villagers, was destroyed on the 3rd of April, 1999. Therefore, it wasn't on the 28th of March, as you stated.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a single person in Rugova village on the 3rd of April; only the animals were still there. You expelled Rugova village on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popaj. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, my learned colleague Mr. Visnjic made a proposition to you that your brother, Nesim Popaj, actually died at another date and at another location than you testified about. Did you bury your brother Nesim with your own hands?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I buried him with my own hands. They were referring to Mesim Vebi Popaj, Vebi being the father's name, who is still alive. Mesim is born in 1965, while the other person still lives. My brother's name was Nesim and the other person's name is Mesim. I buried my brother with my own hands. I put the bottle with his name inside, and when we exhumed him, the bottle was still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Now, my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman asked you about the number of cattle in your village, being 5.000, as you confirmed. What happened to these cattle after the 24th of March, when your village was -- when Serb forces came to your village?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 24th of March, or rather, after the 25th of March, around the 30th of March, I would say, they were carrying the cattle in trucks in the direction of Prizren. They killed some of the cattle, but most of them they carried in trucks in the direction of Prizren. But now you still have more than 50.000 cattle in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 5.000; interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. And you also responded to a question of my learned colleague Mr. Lukic regarding the situation in the village between the 25th of March and the 4th of May, that there was looting going on in Bela Crkva and that there were some people from Rahovec involved in that whom you recognised. Did these people from Rahovec wear a uniform or did they wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing civilian clothes. They were armed with automatic rifles. They came in tractors. They took one of my tractors, the make, Ferguson 39, and other vehicles that we had. They looted everything and then they burned the houses. The person in question asked me, called me, and told me that I could go and pick up my truck somewhere near Nis, between Leskovc and Nis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: When these people did the looting in your village, were there also people in uniforms still present in Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The army was above and the police were stationed in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, I think, when you were questioned again about the people who did the shooting along the Belaje river, you referred to this being done by paramilitaries. What do you actually mean by "paramilitaries"? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, a paramilitary is a person who kills and executes people, innocent people, children. They killed children who were only 2 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to go back to the issue that my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think that actually helps resolve the difficulty that is created by the use of the expression "paramilitary" in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're content to leave it at that, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, I'm going back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, let's do it right away, then, here. These paramilitaries you saw at the Belaje river, or however you would call them, they wore uniforms, did they? I think you said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all wearing uniforms, police uniforms. The 12 that were on my side and who I saw, they were all dressed in uniforms, on the right side of the stream.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And I think there was some further questioning about the colours involved in these particular uniforms. Could you try to explain once more what colour these uniforms had.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that the colour was blue camouflage. I call it green. You will not find persons from my village who will use the same word for the colour. But they had this colour of the curtain, camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And by "the curtains," you mean which curtains?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the Judges, these curtains.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect once more that these curtains are blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt. Mr. Popaj, in the English language, the word "paramilitary" refers to someone who is not actually in the army or in the police. It's an important distinction. If you call somebody a paramilitary, he's not actually a member of the official army or the official police force. Now, when you use the expression "paramilitary," is that what you mean to say, that these people are not part of the army, the official army, or the official police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were part of the official police. They were brought there in vehicles. They didn't come there on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller, that was the sort of clarification I was trying to obtain.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I thought it was clear from the first answer he had actually given when he described what paramilitaries meant in his meaning, but that is certainly much clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And just to round this up, is the -- you mentioned some of the people wear bandannas or scarves around their heads. Did they, at the same time, also wear uniforms? And I'm talking about the group of people who shot the villagers at the Belaje stream.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These wearing uniforms, they had bandannas on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to go back to the questions of the positioning of the tanks in your village on the morning of the 25th of March, which was discussed at length with my learned friend Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we call up Exhibit P93, page 11, and maybe this photograph may help to sort out some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, there is an aerial photo, I think, of your village and it is taken from further away, and I'm wondering whether you can figure out on this photograph the streets which would go from your village to Celine, if it is depicted on this photograph. You may need a minute to orient yourself.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you take the pen and draw along the street that you mean.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This road leaves the village and goes to Celine. From this point, Celine is 800 metres far, not even 1 kilometre. It goes to fields. And this one here and this one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And that is what you meant to describe, when you were discussing it with Mr. Ackerman, as the one road that you are aware of going between your village and the Celine village?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this road, while the road that the tanks took to go up to the hill, it's this one. This road takes a turn and then goes to the middle of Celine. The hill is above here, and that's where they positioned themselves. These are the meadows where we took our cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not entirely clear still. The second road, the lower red line you draw, this is another road which also goes to Celine but via the mountains. Is that what you're saying or --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This road takes you to Rahovec, Nagavc. There is no road that goes to the hill - they climb that hill through the fields - while this road here takes you to Rahovec. And they went to the hill which is above Celine and Nagavc.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So just to be crystal clear, which of the two roads that you've marked did the tanks take, the upper or the lower in the picture?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The upper, the upper road. They went through this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: By "upper," I mean upper in the photograph. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there another --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, on the photograph, it's the lower one, while in the village, it's the upper one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph it's the one below.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't clear in my question at all here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I ask just one thing. And that road, you say, goes to Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it goes to Rahovec. It's not an asphalt road. It's an off-road usually used by us to carry grapes and other sorts of things. It takes you straight to Rahovec. There is a road of Pojata, as we call it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What other place does that road go through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It takes you to Rahovec, to Brestovc and nowhere else; up to Brestovc village, Rahovec, and up to Hoqe e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we take a snap-shot of this picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, there was also some discussion about --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe -- I don't know. I'm concerned about page 58, line 4 and 5. Does that need to be clarified or not? I mean, we've got two different things now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at that stage it was clear to me that he was referring to the road that's the lower one on the map. There was then some confusion following that because of his understanding of what was meant by "lower" and "upper. " And when an attempt was made to clarify that, he said it was the lower road on the photograph. Now that meant to me that he had given two consistent answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think - and I'm quite certain I'm right - the upper red mark that he made was when he was asked to show us the road that goes to Celine. The lower red mark that he made on the photograph, the longer one, was the mark he made when he was showing us where the tanks went. And he says "this road." While the road that the tanks took go up to the hill, it's this one. And that's the one he drew on the bottom, and said this road takes a turn and goes to the middle of Celine. And that gets us back to what the map shows of two roads going to Celine. So I don't know it. I think it's more confused than it was before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This road does not take you to Celine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Popaj. Ms. Moeller, I think it would pay dividends to try and clarify the part of the transcript Mr. Ackerman has identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, if we could -- do we have IC100 -- yes, we still have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, could I ask you to put a number 1 at the street that you lined, which leads from Bela Crkva to Celine, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And could you put a number 2 where you lined the other road.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, when the tanks left your village on the morning of 25 March, did they take road number 1 or road number 2, and just tell us the number?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we take another snap-shot of this, please. I think it's clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up from the same exhibit page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: There was some discussion about where the house of Mr. Fetoshi was located in the village, and where the houses were which were burned first on the 25th of March. And I would like you to have a look at the picture, which comes up next, and tell us whether you can see the Fetoshi house and the area where the houses were first burned on this picture or not.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the house of Fehmi Fetoshi because not everything is included in this shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Are any of the houses which were burned first visible in this picture, or are they also outside of this frame?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know which of the houses were burned down first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher would assist the witness; he's looking for the pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the entrance to the village, when they entered here, they burned these houses first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You have to make -- to draw on the screen again to make it visible, please

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He has done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I didn't see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you also mark the street along which they entered the village; draw a line along it, please.

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we take another snap-shot, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we now call up page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, would Mr. Fetoshi's house be visible on that picture?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- oh, on this one. Hang on a second. You can see a bit of it on the edge here. You can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you indicate the direction where you can see the bit. Only if you can, I mean, if it's outside, don't --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it. It's outside the frame. I don't think the picture shows everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. If you cannot do it then --

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- I'll leave it here. Now, that's fine, Mr. Popaj. Thank you. My last question would be related to the book Fenikset e Lirise - and excuse my pronunciation, please - in which some of your family members are listed. Did you ever see this book before it was shown to you by an investigator in June 2005?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw it first when he came to my house. I heard from other people that it had been written, but I only saw it on that particular day when it was shown to me. And I didn't know on that day that it was an investigator from this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did ever have anyone come to your house and inquire about your son Shendet and your brother and other persons, whether they were actually in the KLA or not, before this book was published or in relation to this book?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one asked me, with the exception of that person who came to ask questions of me and who showed me the book, and I don't even know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And your youngest son who was not even 14 when he was killed, did he ever talk to you about signing a list of the KLA in school?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agon, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in 1998, did your son not tell you that he put his name on a list which was circulated in his school?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have an investigator's notes here that said that he inquired you about Agon - that's the one I'm talking about - and that you told him that your son told you that, in 1998, a list was circulated in his school and that he, among other boys, signed this list, and that you didn't take that serious at the time because he was so young. Do you recall that you said that to the person who came to talk to you about the Fenikset e Lirise book, or not?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. Maybe he told me that, but I cannot remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the roads, Mr. Ackerman, is there anything else you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it would complicate it further, Your Honour. I think we better leave it where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Popaj, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal again to give evidence. You are now free to leave -- oh, I'm sorry, a moment. Judge Nosworthy does want to ask you a question. Sorry. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Popaj, you have said that your son Agon, at 14, and your other son, respectively, at 17, they were too young, in your consideration, to be members of the KLA/UCK. What I want to know from you: As far as your knowledge goes, at what age would young men have joined or been recruited into the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 18 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about when they, themselves, volunteered, as it was alleged that your younger son did?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never left the house. They were there all the time. He went to school every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I understand that that is what you are saying, but does the age of 18 apply equally to when a young man would volunteer for joining the KLA, as it was alleged that your younger son had volunteered?

utterances.speaker: SABRI POPAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time of the former Yugoslavia, I applied to go and serve my military service at 17. It was rejected. I did serve my military service there after 18, after completing 18 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that does now complete your evidence, Mr. Popaj. Thank you for coming. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you from all -- everybody from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are a number of administrative matters it might be appropriate to deal with in the time we have. We'll be breaking around a quarter to 1.00. Mr. Visnjic, can I ask you, you have a 54 bis application for material from the Government of the United Kingdom. They have applied for an extension of time to respond to that, and in that application, which I hope you've received, they say that there are ongoing discussions about material. I notice that on the Prosecution's latest list of witnesses to the end of the year, Colonel Crosland doesn't appear. Now, the question for me is -- for you, rather, is whether there is any point in delaying taking a decision in this matter, or whether, as far as you're concerned, it's got to the stage where the Trial Chamber has to make a decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm getting no interpretation for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] We have already today answered in writing, and I suppose that our filing is somewhere in the pipeline from the Registry towards the Trial Chamber. But I can say briefly that I am not opposed to this extension for the UK on the condition that we get the material before the testimony of Colonel Crosland. And I believe this postponement -- in fact, this new list is precisely intended at finding a convenient time for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter is an application on behalf of Mr. Lukic to bar certain testimony from the scheduled next witness Mehmet Mazrekaj. Now, in view of the fact that the witness is about -- at least is listed to give evidence next, there's no time, obviously, for a written response to this. The application is confined to the question of rape and sexual assault. Now, what response do the Prosecution wish to make to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I think the application raises questions of fairness in terms of adequate notice about the allegation made by the witness. That allegation or that statement was made during proofing recently, and it was transmitted to the Defence at the earliest opportunity, or soon thereafter. It was not in a supplemental information sheet, but the information was in the witness notification, an addendum to the witness notification, in which it was indicated that we would seek to lead that evidence. The application, I think, quite rightly raises the issue as to whether or not they should be notified as to his source of information. I think that is the pith of the argument, that they were not notified as to the source of his information. And we have supplied that information to the Defence -- actually, he was told -- the source is that he was told about the rapes by women who were present in the case where these rapes were committed. That information, being what it is, I don't know if -- or the extent to which that would impact on the preparation the Defence would need to make for cross-examination. So I wonder if the application is being pressed now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what you've said suggests that you don't think the information itself is worth very much, because if you do, then you would expect the Defence to want to investigate and challenge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not saying it is not worth very much. The question is whether or not the source of the information, being what it is, it would impact on the challenge in respect of this particular witness. There would be some limitations to what they could do with this particular witness if they wanted to challenge that allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it's being suggested that you might not be pressing this application.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are pressing this application, Your Honour. We don't file any application that we feel not to be pressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's just impossible for us to assess the implications of allowing this evidence to be led. There has been more than ample time for these matters to be fully investigated by the Prosecution before the start of this trial, and to raise this matter at this stage is, in our view, quite inappropriate. It's unfair to the Defence to allow this particular witness to speak on these matters in the way described by Mr. Stamp, and we therefore will grant this application and we will refuse to admit any evidence about sexual assault or rape that the Prosecution seek to lead from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's another matter with regard to this witness that I'd like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've received the original 65 ter summary - I don't know how long ago, long ago - along with the statement of the witness, and the statement of the witness says nothing about VJ. Then recently we received a new 65 ter summary of the witness containing a paragraph that says: "The witness will testify to these additional matters," where, for the first time, there is mention of VJ. This is becoming highly regular with regard to these witnesses that have nothing to say about the VJ until they arrive here in The Hague and all of a sudden they remember things about the VJ. There are two things about this. First of all, as Your Honour has made clear, we're entitled to rely on the 65 ter summaries that were filed early in this case in terms of our preparation and investigation and whether or not we even care about a particular witness. In addition, on at least two occasions, Your Honour, you have instructed the Prosecution, if they want to amend the 65 ter summary, they need to apply for leave of court to do so. We now have this new summary that, all of a sudden, makes this witness of interest to some of us that was of no interest to some of us earlier, without any application to you for the amendment. And so I think the amendment should not be permitted because there has not been a timely application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which paragraph -- well, I only have the witness notification for the trial week commencing the 30th of October. Is it included there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I can tell you is I have two of them in my book here. One was the one that I think came with the notification for the 30th of October and one that was given to us by e-mail fairly recently, where this additional paragraph was attached down by the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll have a look at that in the break, but I think you face the difficulty in relation to this, Mr. Ackerman, whenever Serb forces are referred to, and that might be seen as enough warning that something may emerge that implicates the VJ. However, I will have a look at the documents in question and indicate the position before the witness starts giving evidence. I want to deal with certain other matters just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I just want to say that I'm concerned about what is the current status of your order, that if they want to amend the 65 ter, they need to apply to you for leave. Is that order no longer valid?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't have an application at the moment so I'm not in a position to make a decision. Let me consider what you've said and obtain the necessary documentation. I want to deal with other matters, because we don't have time to deal with everything at length and there are urgent matters to be dealt with. There's raised with the Trial Chamber the question of the witness Zyrapi and the additional information provided about him and the difficulty that, it's said, will face cross-examiners. Now, who wishes to deal with this for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. Mr. Marcussen will be leading this witness, but I can deal with it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what do you have to say on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we propose that there's certainly adequate information to start cross-examination, and perhaps we'll reach a point where it would be necessary for the Defence to recess to address the additional information they say they need to cross-examine on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's assume, though, that you have other evidence that exhausts this week, what would you do with this witness? Would you still retain him to start at the beginning of next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We would like to do that, rather than send him away and have him come back at a later date, because we are having scheduling difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that raises the question of when we hear the cross-examination of the witness who has returned for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zogaj, Your Honour, he testified on the 21st and 22nd of September. You'll recall he produced a book, I think it was called "Blood Traces" that the Defence hadn't seen and wanted an opportunity to examine and cross-examine him about. We tentatively scheduled him to return on the 25th of October. I had informal discussions with Defence counsel the week before about him coming that week of the 25th, 26th, and 27th, our short week. They indicated they weren't ready, so we put him off to this week. He arrived on Monday and he's been here this week. I really would like to try and get him on and completed so he doesn't have to stay another week or come back a third time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you wanting to take him next?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we proposed to do him after Mr. Mazrekaj, because we thought Mazrekaj would be fairly short and we would have time enough to complete Zogaj, and then whatever time we had left, we might start direct examination of Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does the cross-examination of Mr. Zogaj present a problem for the Defence this week? No. So that problem is resolved, Mr. Hannis. Just a couple of other matters. On the 13th of October, there arose an issue between, I think, Ms. Moeller, representing the Prosecution, and Mr. Ivetic over a number of exhibits, and the parties were instructed and undertook to discuss the position and report back to the Trial Chamber by the following Thursday, which would have been the 19th of October. Nothing's happened on that. There has been an e-mail sent to alert the parties of the failure to do anything about it and still nothing's happened. Now, what is the position? Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can report that I had some conversations with Mr. Ivetic, my learned colleague, just, I think, the day before yesterday. The week before, I think he was out of the country and he signaled that he just hadn't had time to look at the exhumation reports and deaths at the time. But he promised to do that this week and I'm confident that we will be able to let you know maybe early next week, or maybe Mr. Ivetic can speak for himself as to the status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, this morning I had completed looking through the autopsy reports. The situation is as I had expected when the exhibits were tendered: The exhibits tendered are not the complete set of exhibits. The exhibits tendered in particular are photographs that were not led with any witness and do not have any idea -- and we do not have any idea of what the photographs show. Their reference was made to remains that were discovered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell me the time-scale, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can let you know tomorrow what the list of documents that should be tendered if the whole set is tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful. Just, finally, on matters at this stage, also in your case, but possibly being dealt with by Mr. Lukic, a number of exhibits were tendered in untranslated form during the cross-examination of Peraj and there was an order made that a written filing should be submitted once all the translated copies were available. Now, what is the position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have to check on that, Your Honour. As of the other day, I thought we were still waiting on at least one document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again, an e-mail was sent and there's been no response. Now, we expect, at least as a matter of courtesy, if nothing else, that you will respond to these e-mails and tell us the position. It's inappropriate that we should have to take up time here in court to deal with matters which should be capable of being dealt with out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. We will try to follow that in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like an answer to this tomorrow as well. It doesn't necessarily need to be done in the courtroom; it can be done directly to Mr. Dawson, who's been communicating with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, just before we move on, because Mr. Popaj completed the evidence for the murder site of Bela Crkva and there are two exhibits, and it fits in with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll deal with it when we come back, because I think we've already overrun long enough before the interpreters need a break. So I will deal with this afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 1.00 and we will sit until about five past 2.00. When we resume, we will be without Judge Nosworthy, who's committed to the other trial, and we wish to make use of such additional time as we can to compensate for what was lost this morning. So we will resume at 1.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, you were going to raise something about the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. With your leave, I would like to tender Exhibits P93 and P97, which are the crime scene photograph report and the exhumation reports from the Metropolitan Police relating to Bela Crkva. Both exhibits have been addressed with Mr. Popaj and earlier also with Mr. Zhuniqi, who testified about Bela Crkva. We have now concluded our evidence on this particular site. The exhibit P97 was discussed in terms of admission also when Mr. Zhuniqi testified on the 27th of September, 2006, and it is transcript page 4137, lines 6 to 17, and at this stage I ask -- I didn't tender Exhibit P97, but you said that, as far as it was related to by Mr. Zhuniqi, that you would want to make use of it in the transcript. I checked it in e-court; it's not yet admitted. But I just wanted to direct you to this passage in the transcript where the admission was discussed. At this point I seek to tender both exhibits in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any opposition to that, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as to the photographs, we have no objection whatsoever; but as for the report regarding Bela Crkva, I think it contains exhumation reports which, as I understood it, the Prosecution intended to introduce through the expert. Since the issue of the expert is still outstanding, my position now is that I object to the introduction of these reports through witnesses, either Popaj or Zhuniqi, because neither of them have much to do with the expert report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I read this as an application similar to one that's been made before in relation to forensic science material and see the Prosecution as tendering these on their own, in the light of all the other evidence that has been submitted. These ones are being submitted in the context in which it is possible to make sense of them. You have an indication from the Prosecution that they'll be calling the forensic expert Baccard, I think, and I know that you want to cross-examine him on certain aspects of some of the material. In the end of the day, it's going to be a matter of weight, because these ones do fit into the other evidence in a way that we can understand. So the Chamber's attitude to these is to admit them as documents in their entirety. However, this is a suitable opportunity also to deal with an earlier situation. On the 18th of October, at the end of the evidence of the witness Kadriu, the Chamber was invited to admit a number of documents as free-standing documents, as it were, from the bar table. The situation with them is different. This is where the matter you just mentioned originally arose, Mr. Visnjic, the question of cross-examination of an expert. We tend to regard that as a separate issue, albeit an important one. And even if the Prosecution, for some reason, didn't call the expert, you could, of course, call him yourself. And, indeed, it may weaken the Prosecution position in their case in-chief if they haven't called him, I suppose. But this particular set, which was P331 to 334, P206, 210, and P2235, are rather different from the ones we've just been looking at. It's not possible to make proper sense of them in the context of the evidence so far and therefore we do not think that they ought to be admitted as free-standing documents, with one exception. P2235 has already been admitted. It's actually the 92 bis package of Fuad Haxhibeqiri, and it would appear that that -- and it's page 4 of that where there's an issue over identification of policemen, which appears already to have been admitted. But in relation to the others, that's P331 to 334 and P206 and P210, we refuse to admit these at this stage. It may be appropriate to renew the application when other evidence would allow the Chamber to make sense of these exhibits, but that remains to be seen. Now, that takes us to the question raised by Mr. Ackerman. I have now seen the supplemental information sheet for the first time. Now, who is dealing with this witness of the Prosecution? Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the reference that seems to be causing concern is, I think, the second paragraph of this, about the presence of VJ vehicles and soldiers of the VJ in Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what date does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This relates to the dates the 27th to the 29th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you clarify for me the date on which it is said that the witness crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness crossed the border much later than that. I think the witness crossed the border in April - I'm not sure of the date - 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can you tell me on which page of the statement this part would fit in?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He describes the circumstances that obtained while he and other villagers were refugees in a village by the name of Beleg, and he refers to an APC and military vehicles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the current reference to that in the existing -- in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to fit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to fit it into his evidence to see the implications it would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The references to his time in Beleg is really from page 4 of his statement, onwards, to about page 7. But on page 7, in particular, he refers to an APC in a situation that is not entirely clear whether he is reference to one APC or more than one. He says he recognised one of the policemen who was inside the APCs, but it's "APC" with a "comma S." So the question is really whose APC, and how many APCs there were, APC being an armoured vehicle. And the answer to the question is that they were APCs -- armoured vehicles belonging to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the reference to the 18 soldiers being killed is in the statement at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is, though, the separate matter of how this sort of situation should be handled. If you consider it necessary to amend the 65 ter summary, then that's got to be done formally. But it would appear, in this instance, you haven't considered that necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I was of the view that it was really a matter of notice to the Defence. If the witness notification indicates that the Prosecution would move to lead evidence in respect to additional matters, then the application -- and I think Your Honour did suggest that the application could be made orally when the witness comes to testify, the important thing being that notice is given to the Defence that the Prosecution intends to seek to lead that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but do you consider this to alter your 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are references to soldiers and there are references to vehicles, in which the natural question would arises whose vehicle, if it is an armoured vehicle, it is. And therefore, in my estimation, it is not something so entirely new as, for example -- well, without giving examples, it is not something so entirely new as to necessitate a change; however, the -- or an application to amend the 65 ter summary. However, the -- and I know an abundance of caution is not necessarily a good reason. But I would say, since the matter is not entirely beyond debate, the Prosecution, out of caution, would seek to amend or would move to amend, just to be able to lead this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you were referred to various pages of this document. The statement of the witness never mentions VJ, except for that one. You might be able to take it out of the 18 Serb soldiers who were killed causing the roads to be blocked, but that has nothing to do with what's been added to the Rule 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's in the same context, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it's not. What we're talking about is -- we're told, in the new 65 ter, that when they went to Beleg, there were Serb police and VJ personnel and paramilitaries there. When you look at his statement, what it says, they went there on -- about 4.00 p.m., I think, on Saturday; on Sunday, the 28th, then he says some police arrived to check the village. And you've been referred to page 7, that that little statement where he mentions an APC should alert us that that has to do with the VJ, when we know that the police have APCs, and, in fact, the statement is "recognised one of the policemen who was inside the APC." So it's clearly a police APC that's involved. There's nothing there. If you go to the next page, again, it talks about policemen and paramilitary. Never does it say anything about Serb soldiers except that one spot. And then, all of a sudden, at the last minute, we're hit with this thing about VJ personnel being in the village. That's the first time it's ever showed up by implication or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things that guides us -- has guided us in the past also is whether it's realistic to exclude parts of witnesses' evidence. We've made a decision a short time ago to do so because it's clearly separable evidence and it's something that you can do without, putting unrealistic barriers in the way of the witness. This is rather different. We're very sympathetic to Mr. Ackerman's submission that this is the result of inadequate preparation of the Defence case and inadequate efforts by the -- inadequate preparation of the Prosecution case and inadequate efforts to give full details of that case to the Defence during the pre-trial phase. But we're also conscious that this is the sort of material that would probably have emerged in the examination of the witness without notice being given to the Defence that it was going to happen. So I know that it's little consolation to have our sympathy, Mr. Ackerman, but this is one where we will grant the application to extend the 65 ter summary and allow this evidence. But when we've done that in the past, we've made it clear that if it does cause any prejudice, then we will be sympathetic to an application for delayed cross-examination or for re-call, if necessary, of the witness. Mr. Stamp, there's going to come a time when pressure will be such - that's the pressure of the clock will be such - that we won't be able to allow this sort of thing. We'll have to do something which we find distasteful, which is take an otherwise unrealistic approach to a witness's evidence and exclude things in fairness because time will not allow us the luxury of re-call or delay of cross-examination. So we urge you again to think about how you are carrying out these proofing exercises and how much time or notice you're giving the Defence as a result of doing so at the very last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have taken serious steps to try to have the proofing done as early as possible, including utilising what is suggested by Your Honour, the facilities of teleconferencing. Sometimes it just proves impossible to do so with some witnesses, especially when we bring forward witnesses who we had intended to call much later. But we do -- I do accept the sentiments expressed by the Court and we will amend our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please bring in Mr. Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. As I hope you're aware, we already have your statement before us, so we have been able to read the evidence you have provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. The purpose of bringing you here was to enable counsel for the parties to ask you additional questions that they feel are important to assist us to reach the right conclusion in this case. It's important, therefore, to concentrate on the particular issues that the parties raise with you and to try to confine your answers to the particular points you are asked about. The first person or the first counsel to ask questions of you will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you state your name, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: My name is Mehmet Mazrekaj, from the village of Drenoc, municipality from Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Mazrekaj, I understand that on the 4th of February, 2000, you gave a statement to a member of the ICTY Prosecution team in respect to events that occurred in your village of Drenoc in 1998 and 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And are the contents of that statement true; in other words, would your answers remain the same if you were asked about the same matters again or today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Further, on the 18th of September, 2004, you attended before an attesting officer of this Tribunal in Irzniq, in Kosovo, where you attested to the correctness of this statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The statement, Your Honour, is P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your statement you refer to events which you call the first offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to the fourth full paragraph of page 3 of the English copy, and that is also the fourth full paragraph in the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would object to testimony about the first offensive because it all has to do with 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I can't see any relevance to it. Maybe Mr. Stamp can advise you of the relevance that would make it relevant to the indictment, but I don't see the relevance and, therefore, I object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to ask one question because the statement doesn't tell precisely when. It refers to 1998 and the question was when, precisely, did these events occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The events which you describe as the first offensive in your statement, when did they occur?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expect Mr. Stamp to tell us whether this is a 92 bis witness or an 89 witness or whether he's a viva voce witness - I haven't heard all this - and what issues in the indictment he's testifying to. It was my fault, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Actually, it's on the witness notification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is, but you better tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. The witness is 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Formerly, it had been applied under 92 bis (B). And he refers to events in Decani, and that is particularly paragraph 72(l) of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When I say "Decani," I mean the municipality of Decani. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. The events which you describe as having occurred during the first offensive, when did these events occur?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: On May the 29th, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said that as a result of these events you left Albania and thereafter decided to return to Kosovo -- sorry, you said as a result of these events, you left Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- sorry, you went to Decani, in Kosovo, from your village, where you spent some months there and then returned to your home in Drenoc eventually. When did you return to your home in Drenoc?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: We returned to Drenoc three months after first leaving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now could you deal with the objection that's been made, Mr. Stamp? Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Mazrekaj, until I hear from counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure which objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection is that the evidence about 1998 is irrelevant to the indictment, and Mr. Ackerman is asking which part of the indictment you suggest it's relevant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just establishing where the witness was, that he returned to his home at some point and he was living there at a particular point in time. I intend to move on now from that part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but the evidence is there in the written statement and the objection is being taken to that part of the written statement, so the point that's being made is: Is it relevant to the indictment? Mr. Ackerman, is there something else you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it looks to me like Mr. Stamp agrees with me, and in that event, I think if we look at page 2, "When the war started ..." and basically go from page 4 down to right after, "Later nothing had happened because the OSCE was here ..." that that would take out the 68 material. And I'd simply ask that the Trial Chamber exclude that material from your consideration of the testimony of this witness. I don't think we need to go through a formal redaction or anything, unless you believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I, at no point, conceded or suggested that it was not relevant; it's just that I did not intend to go over it or spend time in court to deal with it, except to establish a date. But this is a matter which is part of the -- referred to in the background sections of the indictment, particularly, at paragraph 95 of the indictment, which refers to various operations in 1998, particularly where it says that, "By the end of September, forces of the FRY and Serbia shelled and burned down about half of the villages in Decani municipality." This is what the witness speaks about in that section of his statement. So it is relevant to the indictment, Your Honour, but I did not really want to use time to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in none of the 65 ter notices does paragraph 95 appear as a relevant indictment paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm finding difficulty understanding is the part at the foot of page 2, "When the war started ..." Now, that seems to refer to the beginning -- well, the month of March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would -- it does; that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but you then have the paragraph that you directed attention to, which tells us that the first offensive was in May 1998. So I find this whole section incomprehensible at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the problem with the statement. The statement begins by referring to something which occurred, "the movement of the Serbs in the war started," and then it proceeds, in the last line of page 2, to speak about Serb forces surrounding the village and details of what happened, and concludes by saying that was the first offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is why I just wanted to clarify with the witness what period he is speaking about, with the statement as is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, to leave these statements in this state from the year 2000, six and a half years ago, and present them now in this state, to this Tribunal, runs a very serious risk of a grave injustice being done. It's not fair to the witness to present them in this disorganised state; it is unlikely to give the best presentation of his evidence, and, in accumulation of these statements of a similar nature, it is likely the Prosecution case is not going to be presented in the best light. If that is the case, if that's what happens here, it is going to be a tragedy for which the Prosecution will bear a very grave responsibility. This sort of evidence should be capable of presentation in a simple form, if adequate steps had been taken to put it in order, before these witnesses were presented to us. Carry on with this evidence. We will make a decision about the objection at the end of the evidence, once we see how it can possibly -- we can possibly fit pages 2 to 4 into the overall evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I just, very briefly, Your Honour, call your attention to the last paragraph of the part that I highlighted for you. You'll see that he begins there with, "When the war started ..." and that section I outline ends with, "Later nothing had happened because the OSCE was here..." In other words, he's describing matters that happened before the arrival of OSCE, and then when OSCE arrives, nothing happens after that. And then the next event, we finally go to March of 1999. So that's clearly 1998 material all the way through there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's your interpretation which you may present to us in due course, if the passage remains there. If Mr. Stamp wishes to clarify it, that's for him. Or he may tell us he agrees with that. I don't know if he actually knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the witness has just indicated that the events which he just described in that part of his statement occurred in March 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what war are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He refers to the war on page 2 of his statement, and then -- that is the war in 1999, and then he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you conclude that that's the war in 1999? "Up until then, there were no conflicts between the Serbs and Albanian population in the village," how could that possibly be referring to 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're about to tell us about the conflict between Serbs and Albanians in 1998, how could a passage that says, "When the war started ..." and then goes on, "Until then, there were no conflicts between Serb and Albanian population in the village," how could that be right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The statement, Your Honour, I agree, deals with these issues not in a proper sequential order, which is why all I want from the witness is just to get the dates of when certain things occurred, because it deals with one matter which seems to be 1999, and then it goes back to 1998 and then it comes back to 1999, which is really why I just want to ask him when certain things occurred, because it might not be clear from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in your statement, sir, that when the war started, all the Serbs left the village and went to the town of Decan. Which period are you speaking about when the Serbs left the village and went to Decan?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Serbs who were my neighbours, six families of them. When the offensive started, they left their houses in our village and went and occupied flats in Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is this the period of 1998 when you speak of the first offensive occurring, May 1998, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see from your statement that you're a teacher. As a teacher in the village of Decani --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- did you -- in the village of Drenoc --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- did the villagers select you to take any role or responsibility in respect to the affairs of the village in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was the eldest and so I looked after all the inhabitants of that village, which included the elderly, women, children, and so on, and so I looked after their affairs, to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did they elect you to any position?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The leaders of all the neighbourhoods elected me and I vowed to work on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Elected you to what position?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Some sort of supervisor. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.
